extracted.intended_audience: Federal agency economists and regulatory analysts preparing regulatory benefit-cost and distributional analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for Federal agencies on using income-weighting (distributional weights) in regulatory benefit-cost analyses, including when to use them, how to estimate the income elasticity of marginal utility, data choices, presentation, and robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat income-weighted estimates as primary when less informative
rubrics_metrics.description: “Agencies should not treat estimates using weights that account for diminishing marginal utility as primary if they are less informative about the welfare effects of the regulation than traditionally-weighted estimates.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edited language in Circular A-4 clarifies that income-weighted estimates should not be presented as the primary estimate when they provide less information about welfare than traditional estimates; this is intended to avoid presenting less reliable information to decision-makers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present both traditionally-weighted and income-weighted estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should present both traditionally-weighted estimates and income-weighted estimates of monetized effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB believes presenting both estimates helps explain and relate analysis of a regulation’s monetized effects on social welfare to the policy decision; presentation can clarify when agencies made decisions based on considerations other than social welfare. OMB disagrees that presenting both would necessarily confuse the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income-weighted analysis requires distributional analysis by income
rubrics_metrics.description: Income-weighted estimates rely on measures of benefits and costs stratified by income; if an agency cannot produce a distributional analysis by income, it cannot produce an income-weighted analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB acknowledges empirical and theoretical impediments to producing distributional analyses but reiterates that agencies unable to produce such distributional analyses cannot produce income-weighted analyses. OMB expects analytic and data advances will make such analyses more feasible over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive to weight all benefits and costs consistently; account for implicit weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should "strive to weight all benefits and costs consistently" and, when using population-average WTP/WTA values that may be implicitly weighted, account for those implicit weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters provided step-by-step directions for adjusting income weights when some benefit/cost categories use population averages; OMB finds those materials overly detailed for Circular A-4 but will work with agencies on implementation. Agencies should be careful to identify and adjust for any implicit weighting in input values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use income measures that include taxes and transfer payments
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating income weights, measures of income should include government taxes and payments from transfer programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB agreed with commenters and edited the Circular to explicitly require inclusion of taxes and transfer program payments in the income measure used to compute weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer lifetime income when available; annual income acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure of lifetime income (if available) would often be more informative than an estimate of annual income, but annual income is widely measured and commonly used to estimate the elasticity of marginal utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB recognizes marginal utility depends on more than income and that lifetime income is preferable in many contexts; however, using annual income—because it is widely measured—allows additional insight relative to traditionally-weighted estimates even if imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use absolute value of income elasticity of marginal utility = 1.4 (preferred point estimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB has determined that 1.4 is a reasonable estimate of the absolute value of the income elasticity of marginal utility for use in regulatory analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This estimate was derived from a comprehensive review and meta-analysis (resulting dataset: 1,636 estimates from 158 studies across five lines of evidence) and is reported as 1.37 when listed to two decimal places. OMB describes robustness checks (e.g., U.S.-only gives 1.42; excluding VSL elasticity gives 1.50; other specifications produce 1.6–1.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate income elasticity using multiple lines of evidence and exclude certain evidence for preferred estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop estimates using multiple lines of evidence—including inverse elasticity of intertemporal substitution, Frisch elasticity, relative risk aversion, elasticity of subjective wellbeing measures, and VSL elasticity—and for the preferred estimate exclude expert elicitation and equal-sacrifice income taxation evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB began with Acland and Greenberg (2023) dataset, removed duplicate estimates, added U.S. VSL elasticity studies, and excluded expert elicitation (may reflect experts' normative views) and equal-sacrifice taxation (normative presumption) when constructing the preferred estimate. OMB explains rationale for including/excluding each line of evidence (e.g., concerns about bias or theoretical mapping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include VSL elasticity evidence in the overall evidence set (do not exclude a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence from studies of the income elasticity of the Value of Statistical Life (VSL) is relevant to estimating the absolute value of the income elasticity of marginal utility and should be considered rather than excluded a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some commenters argued VSL elasticity may be upwardly biased relative to marginal utility elasticity under certain theory, OMB finds empirically measured VSL elasticity is not always larger and therefore useful as part of the evidence base; inclusion affects point estimates and robustness checks are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct robustness checks on elasticity estimate by varying country, evidence lines, and trimming extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform sensitivity analyses such as restricting to U.S. studies, adding/excluding lines of evidence (expert elicitation, equal sacrifice, VSL), and excluding extreme percentiles to assess robustness of the elasticity estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB reports resulting estimates under alternative specifications (e.g., U.S.-only: 1.42; include expert elicitation: 1.37; exclude VSL elasticity: 1.50; Acland & Greenberg primary spec: 1.6; trimming extremes or using only micro-data produces 1.6–1.8) and concludes 1.4 is robust to modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the most granular information about benefits and costs, when feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where more disaggregated information would lend insight into overall estimates of benefits and costs, agencies should generally use the most granular information available (all else equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB notes granularity issues affect many analyses (e.g., cumulative exposures, differential effects on subgroups, dose-response functions, geographically disaggregated climate impacts) and that sensitivity to granularity is not unique to income weighting; it supports expanded guidance on producing distributional analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default assumption of comparability at group level; require evidence to rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate default assumption is that individuals are similar to one another on average, so observed evidence on the income elasticity of marginal utility is best explained by commonalities in diminishing marginal utility of income; claims that this assumption does not hold in a regulatory context should be accompanied by supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB endorses the view that distributional weighting requires comparability only at the group level (not individual-level interpersonal comparability), and that any claim that group-level comparability fails should be supported by evidence; this informs when to apply distributional weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presume risk-neutrality; provide guidance on risk-adjustment when WTP/WTA do not reflect preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular A-4 no longer states that an assumption of risk-neutrality is generally appropriate and provides more guidance on how to calculate risk-adjusted benefit or cost values when willingness-to-pay or willingness-to-accept values do not already reflect individuals’ risk preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should adjust monetary measures of benefits and costs for risk preferences when underlying WTP/WTA estimates are not risk-preference-adjusted, rather than defaulting to risk-neutrality; additional guidance is provided in the Circular's treatment of uncertainty section.
